# Google Workspace integration via gogcli — architecture proposal

Status: **implemented** on branch `AF-262-google-workspace-integration-for-agents-via-gogcli`
(2026-08-17), with the deviations listed below. gogcli was confirmed as the tool after
comparing alternatives incl. Google's official `gws` CLI.
Date: 2026-08-17
## Deviations from this proposal, as built

- **No skill seeding.** The integration ships no skill file; all agent guidance lives in
  the AGENTS.md block (`build_gog_policy_md`), which therefore carries the command
  grammar and a worked example per enabled service.
- **v1 services are gmail, calendar, drive, sheets** (the checklist and the content
  validator share `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_SERVICES`).
- **No `client_json` content field.** The UI parses the downloaded client JSON and
  submits `client_id`/`client_secret`; `credentials.json` is synthesized at
  materialization. Storing the raw file would have duplicated the same secret in two
  shapes.
- **No default-account command.** `gog auth alias set default` cannot work — `default`
  is a reserved alias name — and is unnecessary: gog infers the account when exactly one
  token exists for the client, which is always the case in a pod.

token exists for the client, which is always the case in a pod.
- **gmail full access is three scopes**, not two (`gmail.modify`,
  `gmail.settings.basic`, `gmail.settings.sharing`), and gog appends three identity
  scopes (`openid`, `email`, `userinfo.email`) — both verified against the pinned
  v0.37.0 source rather than the docs.
- **Pinned gog v0.37.0**; the release tarball's member is `./gog`, which the Dockerfiles
  extract by that exact name.
- **`hermes-base` now creates and chowns `/home/hermes`.** The Hermes user's home is
  `/opt/data` (the PVC) and `/home` is root-owned and empty upstream, so the intended
  ephemeral `GOG_HOME` was not writable by the agent until the image provided it.
  Verified by running the generated setup script as the unprivileged user in both images.

## Goal

Give agents access to the user's Google apps (Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Docs, Sheets, …)
through [gogcli](https://gogcli.sh) (`gog`, github.com/openclaw/gogcli — "Google Workspace
in your terminal", from the same OpenClaw ecosystem as our agent runtime). The user does
one-time manual setup in Google Cloud Console to obtain an OAuth client JSON; the platform
takes that file, obtains authorization, and provisions agent pods so `gog` works as the
user's account.

### How gog authenticates (docs + source, verified)

- `gog` needs two things: an **OAuth client JSON** (`credentials.json`, installed via
  `gog auth credentials <file>`; both `installed`/Desktop and `web` client types are
  accepted — `internal/config/credentials.go`) and a **refresh token per account email**,
  stored in a keyring under key `token:<client>:<email>`.
- Container/headless recipe (documented for Docker/systemd): `GOG_KEYRING_BACKEND=file` +
  `GOG_KEYRING_PASSWORD=<secret>` (encrypted file keyring) + `GOG_HOME=<abs path>` (config
  root). Static Go binary, linux amd64/arm64 release tarballs; also
  `ghcr.io/openclaw/gogcli` image.
- **`gog auth tokens import <path|->`** imports a refresh token directly into the keyring
  (stdin supported). File schema (`internal/cmd/auth_tokens.go`):

```json
  {
    "email": "user@gmail.com",
    "client": "default",
    "services": ["gmail", "calendar"],
    "scopes": ["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.readonly", "..."],
    "refresh_token": "1//..."
  }
  ```

This means **gog never has to run its own OAuth dance in the pod** — a token obtained
  elsewhere can be injected. `gog auth tokens export` produces the same schema.
- Interactive auth (`gog auth add <email> --services ...`) supports headless variants:
  `--manual` (user pastes the redirect URL back) and `--remote --step 1|2` (step 1 prints
  the URL, step 2 exchanges via `--auth-url`), PKCE S256. The redirect URI is
  `http://127.0.0.1:<random-port>/oauth2/callback` (`oauth_flow_manual_redirect.go`,
  valid only for Desktop-type clients), and the persisted PKCE state under `GOG_HOME`
  has a **10-minute TTL** (`manual_state.go`).
- Scopes are derived per service (`internal/googleauth/service.go`), with narrowing flags:
  `--gmail-scope readonly` → `gmail.readonly` (default `full` = `gmail.modify` +
  settings scopes), `--drive-scope full|readonly|file`, calendar `auth/calendar`

settings scopes), `--drive-scope full|readonly|file`, calendar `auth/calendar`
  (readonly variant exists), `--extra-scopes` for additions.
- **Service accounts with domain-wide delegation** (Workspace only):
  `gog auth service-account set <email-to-impersonate> <sa-key.json>` mints user tokens
  via `google.JWTConfigFromJSON` + subject impersonation
  (`internal/googleapi/service_account.go`) — no per-user consent at all. Requires a
  Workspace admin to enable DWD and grant scopes in the Admin console; does not exist
  for consumer `@gmail.com` accounts.
- Safety surface: runtime guards `--readonly`, `--gmail-no-send`, `--enable-commands`,
  `--disable-commands` (defaults settable in `<GOG_HOME>/config.json`), plus **baked
  safety profiles** (`build-safe.sh safety-profiles/agent-safe.yaml` compiles the policy
  into the binary so flags/env/config cannot loosen it).

into the binary so flags/env/config cannot loosen it).
- gog ships **agent skills** (`.agents/skills/` in the repo, `npx skills add
  https://github.com/openclaw/gogcli`), generated from the CLI schema, plus curated
  workflow skills (inbox triage, meeting prep, drive audit, …).

### Why the OAuth consent cannot happen in the agent pod

- OpenClaw's browser tool is Playwright-backed and defaults to headless when there is no
  display (our pods have none). The docs explicitly direct agents to "report
  login/2FA/captcha … as manual action instead of guessing"; the profiles that permit a
  human to intervene (`user`, `chrome` extension) attach to a browser on the *user's*
  machine, which doesn't exist in a k8s pod. Hermes' browsing in our deployment is
  cloud/Firecrawl-backed — same story.
- Even with a browser, the consent step requires the user's Google password/2FA, which
  must never transit the agent, and Google blocks OAuth in embedded/automated browsers.

So the consent has to happen **in the user's own browser**. The platform already owns
exactly this flow: `api/domains/integrations/google_oauth/routes.py` (popup → signed
state → callback → authenticated code exchange → refresh token → Agent Secret). This
revises the original mental model slightly: the app still takes the user's client JSON
and still provides it to the agent, but the *authorization* step happens in the web UI,
not inside the pod. The pod only ever receives a refresh token.

### How integrations materialize today (the pattern we extend)

`start_agent` (`api/domains/agents/service.py`) decrypts per-provider Agent Secrets
(Pydantic content models in `api/domains/agents/models.py`, Fernet-encrypted, one secret
per provider per agent), then:

1. `build_env` → secret material into the pod Secret as env vars,
2. `build_config_toml` + `build_setup_sh` (aai-cli) → ConfigMap entries; `start.sh` runs
   the setup script at boot, piping env into aai-cli's encrypted secret store,
3. per-provider skill markdown mounted via `skills.json`,
4. `build_integrations_policy_md` / `build_tool_context_md` append "what's configured and
   how to call it" to AGENTS.md / TOOLS.md.

The gog integration follows this shape exactly; it adds a parallel artifact builder
rather than bending the aai-cli one.

```
User (browser)                     API                          Agent pod (boot)
─────────────                      ───                          ────────────────
1. Upload own Web-client     ───▶  validate `web` JSON,
   OAuth JSON (default; app-       encrypt, store
   owned client only for
   verified/internal deploys)
2. Pick services + read-only ───▶  derive scope list
   toggle; click "Connect          (mirror of gog's map)
   Google"
3. Consent popup (existing    ◀──  /authorize-url with those
   google_oauth flow, reused)      scopes + openid email
4. Callback → code           ───▶  /token: exchange code,
                                   read email from id_token,
                                   store AgentSecret:
                                   {email, services, scopes,
                                    refresh_token, client json?}

refresh_token, client json?}
                                                                5. start_agent injects env:
                                                                   GOG_HOME, GOG_KEYRING_BACKEND=file,
                                                                   GOG_KEYRING_PASSWORD (fresh/start),
                                                                   GOG_CLIENT_JSON, GOG_TOKEN_JSON
                                                                6. gog-setup.sh:
                                                                   gog auth credentials <client json>
                                                                   gog auth tokens import -  (stdin)
                                                                   default account = email

default account = email
                                                                7. agent runs `gog gmail search …`,
                                                                   `gog calendar events …`, etc.
```

### Storage: one new provider

```python
class SecretProvider(str, enum.Enum):
    ...
    GOOGLE_WORKSPACE = "google_workspace"

class GoogleWorkspaceContent(SecretContent):
    email: str                    # gog tokens are keyed by account email
    services: list[str]           # gog service names the user authorized
    scopes: list[str]             # exact scopes granted (from token response)
    refresh_token: str
    read_only: bool = False       # which scope variants were requested
    client_id: str = ""           # empty → app-owned client backfilled at start
    client_secret: str = ""       #   (same convention as GmailContent)
    client_json: str = ""         # verbatim uploaded JSON when user brought their own
```

- The consent flow must also learn the **account email** (gog needs it as the token
  key): add `openid email` to the requested scopes and decode the `id_token` in
  `/token`, returning `email` alongside `refresh_token`. Record the `scope` field of
  the token response so the stored `scopes` list reflects what was actually granted.
- Follows the existing rule: OAuth-based providers are excluded from Shared Credentials.
- `_backfill_google_client_credentials` extends to this provider (or synthesizes a
  `{"web": {...}}` client JSON from config when `client_json` is empty).

### Runtime materialization

New `gog_artifacts.py` beside `aai_cli_artifacts.py`:

- **Env** (pod Secret): `GOG_KEYRING_BACKEND=file`, `GOG_KEYRING_PASSWORD`
  (`secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`, fresh per start), `GOG_HOME` (per runtime, see below),
  `GOG_CLIENT_JSON` (uploaded JSON verbatim, or synthesized from client id/secret),
  `GOG_TOKEN_JSON` (the import schema above, built from the content model),
  `GOG_ACCOUNT_EMAIL`.
- **Setup script** (`gog-setup.sh` ConfigMap entry, invoked from both runtimes' start.sh
  next to the existing aai-cli-setup.sh hook):

  ```sh
  rm -rf "$GOG_HOME" && mkdir -p "$GOG_HOME"
  umask 077
  printf '%s' "$GOG_CLIENT_JSON" > /tmp/gog-client.json
  gog auth credentials /tmp/gog-client.json && rm -f /tmp/gog-client.json
  printf '%s' "$GOG_TOKEN_JSON" | gog auth tokens import -
  gog auth alias set default "$GOG_ACCOUNT_EMAIL"
  ```

- **`GOG_HOME` placement — deliberately ephemeral** (container fs, *not* the PVC):
  OpenClaw `/home/node/.config/gogcli` (only `~/.openclaw` is PVC-backed), Hermes
  `/home/hermes/.config/gogcli` (its PVC is `/opt/data`). The keyring is recreated on
  every boot from the injected token, so the password can rotate freely per start, and
  removing the credential removes pod access on next restart with nothing lingering —
  same reasoning as hermes start.sh pruning `/workspace/skills`.
- **Images**: bake the pinned `gog` release tarball into `openclaw-base/Dockerfile` and
  `hermes-base/Dockerfile` (same pattern as the aai-cli binary; add to smoke-test.sh).

### Agent guidance

- Mount gog skill docs the same way aai-cli skills mount: seed a built-in skill row
  whose required provider is `google_workspace`, so configuring the secret auto-mounts
  it. Source the skill content from gog's generated service skills (pinned to the baked
  CLI version) rather than hand-writing command references — they regenerate from
  `gog schema --json`, which keeps docs aligned with the binary.
- AGENTS.md: the existing integrations block says "aai-cli is the only way … always pass
  `--profile`", which is wrong for gog. Add a parallel **Google Workspace (gog)** block
  (own builder, like `build_local_tools_policy_md`): the account email, enabled services,
  `gog <service> <verb>` grammar, read-the-skill-file pointer, and the same no-browser /
  no-invented-URLs policy line.

### Safety layering (strongest first)

1. **Scopes at consent time** — enforced by Google server-side regardless of what the
   agent executes. The UI read-only toggle maps to gog's readonly scope variants
   (`gmail.readonly`, `calendar.readonly`, `drive.readonly`). This is the real boundary.
2. **`<GOG_HOME>/config.json` defaults** written by the setup script (`readonly`,
   `gmail_no_send`, `disabled_commands`) — honest-agent guardrails, since the agent can
   rewrite the file or pass flags. Map `gmail_no_send` to the agent's approval mode.
3. **Baked safety-profile binary** (optional later hardening): `build-safe.sh
   safety-profiles/agent-safe.yaml` produces a binary whose policy can't be changed by
   flags/env/config. Costs a Go build stage in the base images; skip for v1.
## Decisions made, and what the other choices would look like

**D1 — Where OAuth consent happens: platform web UI (reusing the existing popup flow).**
- *In-pod browser*: ruled out — headless pods, Google's automated-browser blocks, and the
  user's password/2FA would have to pass through the agent.
- *Chat-relayed `--manual`/`--remote` flow* (agent posts the auth URL in Slack/Telegram,
  user consents, pastes the redirect URL back): genuinely works headless and is
  gog-native, needs zero new backend code, and lets BYO users bring the simpler
  Desktop-type client. But authorization codes would sit in chat history, the PKCE
  state times out (~10 min), every re-auth is a conversation, the token would need a
  custody story (pod-only keyring on the PVC, or an upstream-to-API endpoint), and it
  breaks the platform pattern where credentials are configured in the UI before start.
  Worth keeping in the back pocket as a fallback UX; not the default.

Worth keeping in the back pocket as a fallback UX; not the default.
- *User runs gog locally and uploads a `gog auth tokens export` file*: zero OAuth code
  on our side, but forces every user to install gog and shepherd a secrets file through
  an upload form. Could be added later as a power-user escape hatch — the content model
  already stores exactly the export schema.
- *Service account + domain-wide delegation* (Workspace orgs only): the only true
  zero-user-intervention option — an admin-provisioned SA key impersonates any domain
  user, no consent step ever. Useless for consumer Gmail, and the SA key is a
  domain-wide credential for the granted scopes, so it demands stricter custody than a
  single user's refresh token. A compelling later **enterprise mode**, orthogonal to
  the popup flow.

**D2 — Whose OAuth client: user-owned Web client by default; app-owned client only as
an opt-in for verified or Workspace-internal deployments. Revised 2026-08-17.**
An app-owned client cannot be the default: Google caps any app requesting **unverified
sensitive/restricted scopes at 100 grant-users over the lifetime of the project, even
in Production status**, and the cap can never be reset — once hit, new consents fail
outright. Lifting it means OAuth verification (weeks for sensitive scopes; a CASA
Tier 2 assessment taking months, recurring, for restricted ones like Gmail and full
Drive). This is exactly why gog, GAM, and rclone all instruct users to create their own
client. So the default path is: the user creates their own Cloud project and **Web
application** client (with our callback registered as an authorized redirect URI and

application** client (with our callback registered as an authorized redirect URI and
the per-service APIs enabled — the setup instructions must walk through this), and
uploads the JSON. Their own client means the unverified-app warning is their own app
(click-through-able), the 100-cap counts only their handful of accounts, and API quota
is their own project's. The app-owned client remains supported behind config for two
cases: an operator who has completed Google verification, or a Workspace org running
the platform with an **Internal**-audience app (no verification, no cap, no warning).
Note the same lifetime cap already constrains the existing app-owned client used by
the legacy Gmail/Sheets popup flow — flipping this default sidesteps that exposure for
the new provider rather than fixing it for the old ones. A user-supplied **Desktop**

the new provider rather than fixing it for the old ones. A user-supplied **Desktop**
client JSON still *cannot* redirect to our web app — only loopback — so supporting it
means adding a paste-the-redirect-URL screen (the platform implementing gog's
`--manual` flow, PKCE included); v2 nicety, v1 rejects Desktop JSON with a clear
message pointing at the Web-client instructions (and noting gog's own quickstart
steers to Desktop, which is not what this platform needs).

**D3 — Provider granularity: one `google_workspace` provider, not per-service.** gog's
model is one token covering many services under one consent; mirroring it keeps one row,
one skill mount, one consent, and no flat-namespace collisions. Per-service providers
(the existing Gmail/Sheets pattern) would give finer-grained attach/detach in the UI but
would duplicate the same refresh token across N rows that drift independently — and
re-consent per service is exactly the UX gog exists to avoid. Service selection still
exists, just *inside* the one provider (checklist → scope list).

**D4 — Tool choice: adopt gog rather than extending aai-cli, running gog as MCP, or
using Google's official `gws` CLI. Decided 2026-08-17.**
Extending aai-cli (in-house Rust) to Calendar/Drive/Docs/Slides/Contacts/Tasks is months
of provider work gog already ships, along with generated agent skills and safety
profiles; the cost of adopting gog is a second command grammar for agents (`gog …` next
to `aai-cli --profile …`) and an upstream dependency to track. gog also has an MCP
server (`docs/mcp.md`) — both runtimes speak MCP — which would give typed tools instead
of shell calls, but it diverges from the established CLI+skills pattern, adds a
long-running process per pod, and loses the skill-doc approach that existing agents are
tuned for. CLI first; MCP is a revisit-later.

The strongest alternative was **`gws`** (github.com/googleworkspace/cli — official
Google Workspace CLI, Apache-2.0, Rust, released 2026): commands generated at runtime
from Google's Discovery Service (near-total API coverage), 40+ agent skills, headless
auth via `gws auth export` + `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_CREDENTIALS_FILE`. gog won on:
hard safety rails (`--readonly`, `--gmail-no-send`, command allow/deny lists, baked
safety-profile binaries — gws has fewer documented guards over a much larger generated
command surface), curated commands sized for agent context, OpenClaw-ecosystem
alignment with our runtime, and gws's pre-1.0 "expect breaking changes" status. See
gog's own published comparison (gogcli.sh/gws-comparison.html). Note the architecture
is tool-portable: both CLIs support platform-custody token injection, so a later swap

is tool-portable: both CLIs support platform-custody token injection, so a later swap
to gws would replace the materialization builder and skills, not the consent flow or
storage schema. Also surveyed and ruled out: GAM7/GAMADV-XTD3 (Workspace *admin* tool
— domain-admin credentials, paid Workspace only, wrong shape for act-as-one-user),
single-service baskets (gcalcli, himalaya, rclone, gdrive, clasp — N auth flows and
output formats), and commercial-backend options (Nylas CLI, PortEden).

**D5 — Existing Google providers: coexist, then deprecate the weakest.** `gmail`,
`google_sheets`, `google_calendar` (aai-cli) stay untouched; `google_workspace` is
additive. The UI should discourage configuring both a legacy Google provider and
`google_workspace` on the same agent (double consent, conflicting instructions), without
hard-blocking it. `google_calendar` should be first to fold in: its content model stores
a bare short-lived `access_token`, so it breaks hours after configuration — gog's
calendar service with a refresh token strictly supersedes it.

**D6 — Keyring lifecycle: per-boot re-import on ephemeral `GOG_HOME`.** The alternative
(keyring on the PVC, stable password) would survive restarts without re-import, but the
password would have to be persisted and rotated carefully, stale tokens would outlive
credential removal, and gog's keyring would become a second long-lived secret store to
reason about. Rebuilding from the encrypted DB row on every boot keeps the DB as the
single source of truth — identical to the aai-cli secret-store approach.
## Operational caveats (verify during implementation)

- **OAuth app publishing status drives both token lifetime and the user cap**
  (confirmed against Google's docs, 2026-08): "Testing" status → 7-day refresh tokens
  and a hard 100-*test-user* list; "Production" with unverified sensitive/restricted
  scopes → unverified-app warning plus the **lifetime, unresettable 100-grant-user
  cap**; verification lifts the cap (weeks for sensitive, CASA Tier 2 — months,
  recurring — for restricted scopes like Gmail/full Drive); Workspace **Internal**
  apps skip all of it. The user-client setup instructions must therefore say: set the
  consent screen to Production (or Internal for Workspace) — do not leave it in
  Testing, or tokens die weekly.
- The user's Cloud project must have the per-service APIs enabled
  (`gmail.googleapis.com`, `calendar-json.googleapis.com`, … — gog's map is in

(`gmail.googleapis.com`, `calendar-json.googleapis.com`, … — gog's map is in
  `internal/googleauth/service.go`; `gog auth setup --enable-apis` exists for the
  user-side manual path). With user-owned clients this is part of the standard setup
  instructions; only opt-in app-owned-client deployments ride on the operator's
  project.
- Add a `google_workspace` entry to `PROVIDER_VALIDATORS` that exercises the refresh
  token (token refresh + a cheap API call) so "Validate" in the UI catches expired or
  revoked grants — this is where testing-mode 7-day expiry will surface.
- Pin the gog version in the base images and in the skill-doc generation; `gog auth`
  state formats have changed across versions (the docs warn cross-version manual auth
  breaks).

## Change-impact checklist

Per `docs/features/integrations.md`, a provider addition touches:

| Area | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `api/domains/agents/models.py` | `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE` enum member, `GoogleWorkspaceContent`, registry + display name |
| `api/domains/integrations/google_oauth/routes.py` | scope derivation from `services` + `read_only`, `openid email` scope, return `email` (+ granted `scope`) from `/token` |
| new `api/domains/agents/gog_artifacts.py` | env / setup-script / AGENTS.md-block builders |
| `api/domains/agents/service.py` `start_agent` | decrypt → backfill client → inject gog env + ConfigMap entries |
| `builders/openclaw.py`, `builders/hermes.py`, both `start.sh` | mount `gog-setup.sh`, run it at boot |
| `openclaw-base/Dockerfile`, `hermes-base/Dockerfile` | bake pinned gog binary; smoke tests |
| skill seeding | built-in `google_workspace` skill (generated gog service skills), auto-mount on provider |

| skill seeding | built-in `google_workspace` skill (generated gog service skills), auto-mount on provider |
| UI (`ui/src/features/agents/`, account) | client-JSON upload, service checklist, read-only toggle, connect popup reuse; Zod schemas. Setup help: our own 5-step checklist only (project → enable APIs → consent screen to Production/Internal → **Web** client with our callback → upload JSON); deliberately no link to gog's quickstart, which steers to a Desktop client and omits the Production consent-screen step |
| tests | `test_google_oauth` scope/email cases, `test_agents` materialization, artifact builder units |

# Gmail OAuth 2.0 setup (Google Cloud Console)

One-time setup for the shared Google OAuth client that powers the **"Authenticate with
Google"** button on the Gmail skill. This replaces the old manual client_id/client_secret/
refresh_token entry (see `Gmail, Sheets and Zoho Mail creds generation (for aai-cli).md`) —
end users now just click a button and approve access; only the resulting refresh token is
stored per-agent.

The app-owned client id/secret created here are set once as `GOOGLE_CLOUD_CLIENT_ID` /
`GOOGLE_CLOUD_CLIENT_SECRET` in backend config, never shown to end users.

---

## 1. Create or select a Google Cloud project

Go to `https://console.cloud.google.com/` → create a new project or select an existing one.

## 2. Enable the Gmail API

APIs & Services → **Enable APIs & Services** → search "Gmail API" → **Enable**.

If you skip this step, token exchanges will succeed but API calls will fail with a
`SERVICE_DISABLED` 403 error.

## 3. Configure the OAuth consent screen

APIs & Services → **OAuth consent screen**.

- **User type**: External (unless your org uses Google Workspace and wants Internal-only).
- **App name / support email / logo**: whatever fits your product.
- **Scopes**: add `.../auth/gmail.readonly` (read-only Gmail access — matches what the app
  requests).
- **Test users** (while in Testing mode): add every Google account that needs to connect
  Gmail during development.

### Important caveats

- `gmail.readonly` is a **restricted** scope. Before non-test users can connect, the app
  must pass **Google's OAuth app verification** (a review process that can take days to
  weeks and may require a privacy policy URL, a demo video, etc.). Plan for this before
  launching to real users.
- While the app is in **Testing** mode, Google-issued refresh tokens **expire after 7
  days**, regardless of use. Users will need to reconnect weekly. Move the app to
  **Production** (after verification) for refresh tokens that last until revoked.

## 4. Create the OAuth 2.0 client

APIs & Services → **Credentials** → **Create Credentials** → **OAuth client ID**.

- **Application type**: **Web application** (not "Desktop app" — the redirect-based popup
  flow requires a registered web redirect URI; Desktop-app clients don't support this).
- **Name**: anything recognizable, e.g. "Agent Barn — Gmail OAuth".
- **Authorized redirect URIs**: add one entry per environment, exactly matching
  `<WEB_APP_URL>/api/v1/integrations/google/callback`:
  - Local dev: `http://localhost:3000/api/v1/integrations/google/callback`
  - Production: `https://agent-farm.k8s.aai-labs.com/api/v1/integrations/google/callback`

  The redirect URI must be **byte-identical** between what the backend sends to Google and
  what's registered here — mismatches fail with `redirect_uri_mismatch`.
- Click **Create**. Note the **Client ID** and **Client secret** shown — you'll need both.

## 5. Set the credentials in app config

Add the client id/secret as backend config (never exposed to the frontend or end users):

**Local dev** (`.env`, see `.env.spec`):
```
GOOGLE_CLOUD_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id.apps.googleusercontent.com
GOOGLE_CLOUD_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret
```

**k8s deploy** (`.env` used by `helmfile.yaml.gotmpl`, see `.env.deploy.spec`): same two
variables. They're written into the `agentfarm-api` k8s Secret
(`GOOGLE_CLOUD_CLIENT_ID` / `GOOGLE_CLOUD_CLIENT_SECRET`) and injected into the API pod.

If these are left blank, the "Authenticate with Google" button still renders, but clicking
it returns `503 Google OAuth is not configured on this server.`

## 6. Verify

1. Restart/redeploy the API so the new env vars are picked up.
2. In the UI, hire or edit an agent, assign the **Gmail** skill, and click
   **Authenticate with Google**.
3. Complete the Google consent screen (as a test user, if still in Testing mode) → the
   popup should close automatically and the card should show "Connected".
4. Confirm the agent can use `aai-cli --profile gmail-work` once started (reads the
   refresh token from the stored secret and the client id/secret from config).

---

## Publishing to Production (removing the 7-day token expiry / Testing-mode user limit)

1. OAuth consent screen → **Publish App**.
2. If the requested scopes include any **restricted** or **sensitive** scope (Gmail's
   `gmail.readonly` is restricted), Google requires **verification** before the app can
   serve non-test users in Production:
   - A privacy policy URL and (usually) a homepage.
   - A short screencast demonstrating the OAuth consent flow and how the requested scope
     is used.
   - Optionally a CASA security assessment for higher-risk scopes (not typically required
     for `gmail.readonly` alone, but Google's review team makes the final call).
3. Verification review can take anywhere from a few days to several weeks — budget for
   this before promising the feature to end users outside your test-user list.

# Email Token Refresh

How to provision Google sheets, Gmail and Zoho Mail REST for use with `aai-cli`. The tool automatically exchanges a refresh token for a fresh access token on every request — no manual token rotation needed.

## Gmail

### One-time setup

1. Go to `https://console.cloud.google.com/` → create or select a project
2. Enable the **Gmail API**: APIs & Services → Enable APIs & Services → search "Gmail API" → Enable

   If you skip this step the tool will return a `SERVICE_DISABLED` 403 error even with valid credentials.
3. Go to **APIs & Services → Credentials → Create Credentials → OAuth client ID**
4. Application type: **Desktop app** → give it a name → Create
5. Note your `client_id` and `client_secret`

source: /home/samuel/agent-farm/lessons/Gmail, Sheets and Zoho Mail creds generation (for aai-cli).md
text:
### Get a refresh token (one-time, lasts until revoked)

Run this URL in a browser (replace `CLIENT_ID`):

```
https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth?client_id=CLIENT_ID&redirect_uri=urn:ietf:wg:oauth:2.0:oob&response_type=code&scope=https://mail.google.com/&access_type=offline&prompt=consent
```

Sign in → Allow → copy the authorization code shown on screen.

Exchange it for tokens (replace `CLIENT_ID`, `CLIENT_SECRET`, `AUTH_CODE`):

```
curl -X POST https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token \
  -d client_id=CLIENT_ID \
  -d client_secret=CLIENT_SECRET \
  -d code=AUTH_CODE \
  -d redirect_uri=urn:ietf:wg:oauth:2.0:oob \
  -d grant_type=authorization_code
```

Save the `refresh_token` from the response — you only see it once.

aai-cli --config local/e2e.config.toml secrets set google.gmail_refresh_token --value "REFRESH_TOKEN"
```

### config.toml profile

```
[profiles.gmail-work]
provider = "google"
auth_type = "bearer_token"
client_id = "YOUR_CLIENT_ID.apps.googleusercontent.com"
client_secret_secret = "google.client_secret"
refresh_token_secret = "google.gmail_refresh_token"
user_id = "me"
```

## Zoho Mail REST

### One-time setup

1. Go to `https://api-console.zoho.com/`
2. Click **Self Client** → **Create Now** (if not already created)
3. Note the `client_id` and `client_secret` shown on the Self Client page

### Get a refresh token (one-time, does not expire)

1. On the Self Client page click **Generate Code**
2. Scope: `ZohoMail.accounts.READ,ZohoMail.messages.READ`
3. Time Duration: `10 minutes`
4. Click **Create** → copy the authorization code

Exchange it for tokens (replace `CLIENT_ID`, `CLIENT_SECRET`, `AUTH_CODE`):

```
curl -X POST "https://accounts.zoho.com/oauth/v2/token" \
  -d code=AUTH_CODE \
  -d grant_type=authorization_code \
  -d client_id=CLIENT_ID \
  -d client_secret=CLIENT_SECRET \
  -d redirect_uri=https://api-console.zoho.com/callback
```

Save the `refresh_token` from the response — it does not expire.

provider = "zoho"

```

## Google Sheets

### One-time setup

1. Go to `https://console.cloud.google.com/` → create or select a project
2. Enable both APIs: APIs & Services → Enable APIs & Services → search each name → Enable

## How token refresh works in aai-cli

Every outgoing request automatically:

1. Reads `refresh_token`, `client_id`, and `client_secret` from the profile (via secrets file)
2. POSTs to the provider's token endpoint to obtain a fresh access token
3. Uses that access token for the actual API request

No manual refresh step or cron job is needed. If a stored access token (`token_secret`) is present instead of refresh credentials, it is used directly as a fallback.

# Helm and Helmfile — Fundamental Concepts

## 1. What is Helm?

Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes. Instead of hand-writing and
`kubectl apply`-ing raw YAML, you write reusable, parameterized templates once
and let Helm fill in the blanks and apply the result.

Core concepts:

Core concepts:

- **Chart** — a package/directory containing templated Kubernetes YAML
  (Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, etc.), parameterized with
  variables.
- **Values** — the config inputs that fill in a chart's templates (image
  tags, replica counts, env vars, credentials, etc.).
- **Release** — one deployed instance of a chart with one specific set of
  values. The same chart can be installed multiple times as different
  releases — e.g. this repo's `helm/postgres` chart is deployed twice, as
  `postgres-app` and `postgres-litellm`, each with its own values.
- **Templates** — Go-template YAML files inside a chart that get rendered
  using the values into real Kubernetes manifests, then applied to the
  cluster.

## 2. Charts vs. template files

A **chart** is not a single template file — it's the whole package. A chart
directory typically contains:

- `Chart.yaml` — metadata (name, version)
- `values.yaml` — default values
- `templates/` — the actual Go-template YAML files
- optionally, subcharts (dependencies)

The Go-template YAML files live *inside* the chart, in its `templates/`
folder. "Values get filled into the chart" is shorthand for "values get
filled into the template files that make up the chart." There's one
rendering process: Helm takes the chart (templates + values), renders the
templates using those values, and out comes plain YAML.

## 3. What rendering produces

When Helm renders a chart's templates, the output is plain, fully-resolved
Kubernetes YAML manifests (Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, ...),
with every `{{ .Values.xxx }}` placeholder replaced by an actual value. That
rendered YAML is what Helm sends to the Kubernetes API — equivalent to
`kubectl apply`.

You can preview this yourself without touching the cluster:

```bash
helm template <chart>
```

Key points:

- The leading underscore tells Helm "don't render this as a standalone
  manifest" — Helm skips files starting with `_` when generating output.
- `{{- define "name" -}} ... {{- end }}` blocks declare a reusable snippet,
  callable elsewhere with `{{ include "name" . }}`.
- This is a convention (not a Helm requirement) for centralizing common
  bits — labels, selectors, name-generation logic — so every real manifest
  template (`deployment.yaml`, `service.yaml`, etc.) can `include` them
  instead of repeating the same YAML.

## 5. Where Helmfile fits in

Helm alone only knows how to install/upgrade **one chart at a time**
(`helm install litellm ./helm/litellm --set ...`). This repo has five charts
(`postgres` x2 releases, `litellm`, `agentfarm-api`, `agentfarm-ui`) that must
be deployed together, in dependency order, with values pulled from env vars
and secrets. Doing that by hand with five separate `helm` commands is what
Helmfile replaces.

`helmfile.yaml.gotmpl` is itself a Go-template (hence `.gotmpl`). It lists,
for each release: which chart to use, what values/overrides to pass it, and
what it `needs` (dependency ordering — e.g. `litellm` needs Postgres up
first).

Layering:

**Helmfile (orchestrates multiple releases) → Helm (renders one chart's
templates into YAML and applies it) → Kubernetes API**

## 6. What rendering `helmfile.yaml.gotmpl` produces

Rendering the `.gotmpl` file is a *separate* pass from rendering a chart's
templates. It produces a plain YAML document — the same release-list
structure you see in the source file, but with every `{{ ... }}` expression
(mainly `env "VAR_NAME"` lookups) replaced by its resolved value.

For example, this:

```yaml
set:
  - name: masterKey
    value: {{ env "LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" | required "..." | quote }}
```

becomes:

```yaml
set:
  - name: masterKey
    value: "sk-abc123..."
```

with the real value pulled from the shell's `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY` env var at
the moment `helmfile sync` is run.

with the real value pulled from the shell's `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY` env var at
the moment `helmfile sync` is run.

This resolved release list is Helmfile's internal config — it is **not** a
Kubernetes manifest and is not applied to the cluster directly. Helmfile
reads it and then, for each release, invokes Helm, which does its own
separate template-rendering pass (per chart) into actual Kubernetes YAML.

So there are two distinct rendering passes:

1. Helmfile's own `.gotmpl` → resolved release config (this section)
2. Each chart's `templates/*.yaml` → resolved Kubernetes manifests (section 3)

## 7. The full value chain: shell → live Kubernetes objects

Worked example using the `postgres-app` release:

```yaml
- name: postgres-app
  chart: ./helm/postgres
  values:                      # → becomes -f <rendered-values-block>
    - secretName: postgres-app
      storage:
        size: 5Gi
  set:                         # → becomes --set flags
    - name: storage.storageClass
      value: {{ env "STORAGE_CLASS" | default "" | quote }}
    - name: db.user
      value: {{ env "POSTGRES_APP_USER" | required "..." | quote }}
    - name: db.password
      value: {{ env "POSTGRES_APP_PASSWORD" | required "..." | quote }}
```

**Step 1 — Shell env vars.**
Before running `helmfile sync`, you export `POSTGRES_APP_USER=foo`,
`POSTGRES_APP_PASSWORD=bar`, etc.

**Step 2 — Helmfile's own template pass.**
`helmfile.yaml.gotmpl` is rendered; each `env "POSTGRES_APP_USER"` call pulls
the shell var in. Output: a resolved release entry with a `values:` block
(literal YAML, no `env` calls — e.g. `secretName: postgres-app`,
`storage.size: 5Gi`) and a `set:` list of `{name, value}` pairs with the
shell values substituted in (e.g. `db.user: "foo"`).

**Step 3 — Helm invocation.**
Helmfile shells out to Helm once per release. The two keys become two
different command-line mechanisms:

- **`values:`** → Helmfile writes that block to a temporary YAML file and
  passes it as `-f <temp-file>`.
- **`set:`** → Helmfile turns each `{name, value}` pair into a `--set
  name=value` flag.

Roughly:

```bash
helm upgrade --install postgres-app ./helm/postgres \
  -f <rendered-values-block> \
  --set db.user=foo \
  --set db.password=bar \
  ...
```

**Step 4 — Value merge inside Helm.**
This is where the chart's own `values.yaml` (section 2) enters the picture.
Helm merges three layers, lowest → highest precedence:

1. the chart's built-in `helm/postgres/values.yaml` (defaults, e.g. maybe
   `storage.size: 1Gi`)
2. the `-f` values file from Helmfile's `values:` key (overrides the
   default, e.g. `storage.size: 5Gi`)
3. the `--set` flags from Helmfile's `set:` key (highest precedence, e.g.
   `db.user=foo` sourced from the shell)

The result is one final merged values map for this release.

**Step 5 — Template rendering.**
Helm renders every file in `helm/postgres/templates/*.yaml`
(`deployment.yaml`, `service.yaml`, `secret.yaml`, etc.), substituting
`{{ .Values.db.user }}` → `foo`, and expanding any `{{ include "postgres.labels" . }}`
calls defined in `_helpers.tpl`.

**Step 6 — Apply.**
The resulting plain YAML manifests are sent to the Kubernetes API and
created/updated as real objects (Deployments, Services, Secrets, ConfigMaps)
in the `agent-farm` namespace.

### Summary of the chain

```
shell env vars
  → helmfile.yaml.gotmpl render (env "..." lookups resolved)
  → per-release values: (→ -f file) and set: (→ --set flags)
  → Helm value merge (chart values.yaml < -f file < --set flags)
  → chart template render (templates/*.yaml + _helpers.tpl)
  → real Kubernetes objects applied to the cluster
```

# Local k3s Skill

How to run the entire agent-farm stack on a single-node k3s cluster on your
local machine, using **only locally built images** (no pulls from the AAI Labs
registry). Read this top-to-bottom the first time; skim later for reference.

---

## Why local k3s?

Agents are deployed as Kubernetes Deployments + PVCs + Services. There is no
"in-process" mode for agent lifecycle: starting an agent literally calls the
Kubernetes API to create a pod. To develop or debug the platform you need a
cluster.

Local k3s is preferred over the shared remote cluster because:

- You can rebuild and load images at machine speed (no registry push).
- You can break it freely (`k3s-uninstall.sh` + reinstall in <2 min).
- No SSH tunnel, no shared state, no risk to anyone else's work.
- You can test code paths that touch real PVCs, ConfigMaps, and pod logs.

The **remote** cluster (`k8s.aai-labs.com`, requires SSH tunnel via bastion)
is for production-like work only. If you're tempted to SSH into the bastion
for local development, stop — you almost certainly want local k3s instead.

---

## Local k3s vs remote k3s — which kubeconfig, when to SSH

| | Local k3s | Remote k3s |
|---|---|---|
| **kubeconfig** | `miscellaneous/agent-farm-user-kubeconfig.k3s-local.yaml` | `miscellaneous/agent-farm-user-kubeconfig.local.yaml` |
| **SSH tunnel needed?** | No — cluster runs on this machine | Yes — must tunnel 6443 through the bastion first |
| **SSH tunnel command** | — | `ssh -i miscellaneous/bastion_ed25519 -N -L 6443:10.100.0.11:6443 bastion@k8s.aai-labs.com` |
| **Use for** | All development, rebuilds, debugging | Production-like deploys, CI verification |

Quick test: if `kubectl get pods -n agent-farm` returns "certificate signed by unknown authority",
you have the remote kubeconfig set and the tunnel isn't up. If it returns
"connection refused (localhost:8080)", you have no `KUBECONFIG` set at all.

---

## One-time machine setup

### 1. Install k3s

```bash
curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh -s - --disable servicelb --write-kubeconfig-mode 644
until kubectl --kubeconfig=/etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml get nodes | grep -q " Ready"; do sleep 3; done
export KUBECONFIG=/etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml
```

`--disable servicelb` keeps klipper-lb from grabbing host ports — Traefik
stays (ingress resources install harmlessly) but we never hit it; everything
goes through `kubectl port-forward`.

### 2. Namespace + scoped ServiceAccount

The helmfile expects a kubeconfig pointing at a `ServiceAccount` named
`agent-farm-user` scoped to the `agent-farm` namespace. Create the SA, a
namespace-scoped `Role` granting `*` on `["", "apps", "batch"]` resources, a
`RoleBinding`, and a `kubernetes.io/service-account-token` secret. Wait for
the token to populate before extracting it.

### 3. Build two kubeconfigs from that token

Same token, two different `server:` URLs:

| File | server | Used by |
|------|--------|---------|
| `miscellaneous/agent-farm-user-kubeconfig.k3s-local.yaml` (gitignored) | `https://127.0.0.1:6443` | Your shell, this skill, the helmfile |
| `agent-farm-user-kubeconfig` k8s Secret in the cluster | `https://kubernetes.default.svc` | Mounted into the agentfarm-api pod for `kubectl exec` into agent pods |

### 4. Bootstrap shared secrets

```bash
export KUBECONFIG=/home/samuel/agent-farm/miscellaneous/agent-farm-user-kubeconfig.k3s-local.yaml
bash miscellaneous/bootstrap-secrets.sh
```

Creates: `registry-pull-secret`, `postgres-app`, `postgres-litellm`,
`agentfarm-api`, `litellm`.

Then patch `agentfarm-api` with the extra env vars agent start/stop needs
(not in the production Secret yet because agents haven't shipped):
`AGENT_TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (Fernet), `LITELLM_BASE_URL`,
`AGENT_LITELLM_BASE_URL` (both `http://litellm:4000`),
`AGENT_IMAGE_PULL_SECRET=registry-pull-secret`,
`AGENT_DEFAULT_MODEL=litellm/gpt-5-mini`, `K8S_NAMESPACE=agent-farm`.

### 5. First deploy

```bash
helmfile sync
```

Hooks run in order: `litellm-key-configmap` → `litellm-key-job` (waits for
LiteLLM, calls `/key/generate`, writes the `litellm-api-key` Secret) →
`migration-job` (alembic).

At this point everything is pulled from `registry.k8s.aai-labs.com`. Now we
swap each image for a local build.

---

## Local image workflow — the core idea

k3s ships with **containerd**, not Docker. They have **separate image
stores**. A `docker build` output is invisible to k3s until you bridge it:

```
┌──────────────┐  docker save | k3s ctr images import -  ┌──────────────┐
│ Docker store │ ───────────────────────────────────────▶│ k3s store    │
└──────────────┘                                          └──────────────┘
```

And k3s will only use the local copy if you tell it not to pull from a
registry — set `imagePullPolicy: Never` on the container.

The full loop for any image:

```bash
# 1. Build (run from repo root for api; ui/openclaw-base have their own contexts)
docker build -f api/Dockerfile -t agentfarm-api:local .

# 2. Make it visible to k3s (REQUIRES SUDO — run manually)
docker save agentfarm-api:local | sudo k3s ctr images import -

# 3. Point the Deployment at the local tag with pullPolicy: Never
export KUBECONFIG=/home/samuel/agent-farm/miscellaneous/agent-farm-user-kubeconfig.k3s-local.yaml
kubectl patch deployment agentfarm-api -n agent-farm --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/image","value":"agentfarm-api:local"},
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/imagePullPolicy","value":"Never"}
]'

# 4. Rebuild later? Same build + import + rollout restart (no re-patch needed)
docker build -f api/Dockerfile -t agentfarm-api:local .
docker save agentfarm-api:local | sudo k3s ctr images import -
kubectl rollout restart deployment/agentfarm-api -n agent-farm
```

Important gotchas:

Important gotchas:

- `sudo k3s ctr images import -` **cannot be run from tooling** — sudo needs
  a TTY. Always ask the human to run step 2.
- `imagePullPolicy: Always` (the default in this chart) silently re-pulls on
  every pod restart and falls back to the registry. Make it `Never` for any
  locally built image.
- A `helmfile sync` wipes these patches. After a sync, re-apply them.
- Port-forwards die on rollout restart. Re-establish after every restart.

### Image-by-image specifics

| Image | Dockerfile | Build context | Deployment | Used by |
|-------|------------|---------------|------------|---------|
| `agentfarm-api:local` | `api/Dockerfile` | repo root | `agentfarm-api` | FastAPI backend |
| `agentfarm-ui:local` | `ui/Dockerfile` | `ui/` | `agentfarm-ui` | Next.js frontend |
| `agentfarm-openclaw-base:local` | `openclaw-base/Dockerfile` | `openclaw-base/` | (none) — referenced by `AGENT_IMAGE` env var on the api pod | Every spawned agent pod |

UI build **must** pass `--build-arg NEXT_PUBLIC_BACKEND_URL=http://agentfarm-api:8000`.
Next.js bakes `rewrites()` at build time — if the arg is omitted it falls back
to `http://localhost:8000`, which is the pod's own loopback (not the API service).
Symptom: login returns a **500** immediately. Verify the baked URL with:
```bash
kubectl exec -n agent-farm <ui-pod> -- cat /app/.next/routes-manifest.json | grep destination
```
The correct output is `"destination":"http://agentfarm-api:8000/api/:path*"`.
The browser only sees relative paths because Next.js proxies `/api/*` server-side.

Openclaw base is **not** a Deployment — it's the image used when the api
spawns an agent pod, controlled by the `AGENT_IMAGE` env var on the
`agentfarm-api` Deployment (set from `openclawImage.repository:tag` in
[helm/agentfarm-api/values.yaml](helm/agentfarm-api/values.yaml)). To use a
local openclaw image:

```bash
docker build -t agentfarm-openclaw-base:local openclaw-base/
docker save agentfarm-openclaw-base:local | sudo k3s ctr images import -

kubectl set env deployment/agentfarm-api -n agent-farm \
  AGENT_IMAGE=agentfarm-openclaw-base:local
```

kubectl set env deployment/agentfarm-api -n agent-farm \
  AGENT_IMAGE=agentfarm-openclaw-base:local
```

Then in the agent's pod spec you also need `imagePullPolicy: Never`. This
isn't a deployment patch — the api builds the pod spec in code. The cleanest
local workaround is to set `agent_image_pull_secret` to empty (so no pull
secret) **and** edit `api/domains/agents/builders.py:build_deployment` to add
`image_pull_policy="Never"` to the `V1Container` for local testing only —
don't commit that. (A proper fix is to make it env-driven.)

## Daily access

```bash
export KUBECONFIG=/home/samuel/agent-farm/miscellaneous/agent-farm-user-kubeconfig.k3s-local.yaml

# Port-forward in two backgrounded shells (or use & + nohup)
kubectl port-forward svc/agentfarm-ui 3000:3000 -n agent-farm &
kubectl port-forward svc/agentfarm-api 8000:8000 -n agent-farm &
```

- UI: <http://localhost:3000> — login `admin@agent-farm.com` /
  `d141ximZ3cW!`
- API: <http://localhost:8000/api/v1/health>

Port-forwards are fragile — they die when the target pod restarts. After any
`kubectl rollout restart`, re-establish them. If `curl` returns "Connection
refused", that's almost always the reason.

---

## Agent lifecycle via the API

`/agents` endpoints take a bearer token. Login is form-encoded
(`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`), not JSON:

```bash
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/auth/login \
  -d "username=admin@agent-farm.com&password=d141ximZ3cW!" \
  | python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['access_token'])")
```

| Action | Call |
|--------|------|
| Create | `POST /api/v1/agents` with name + slack tokens + soul/identity md |
| Start | `POST /api/v1/agents/{id}/start` — creates ConfigMap, Secret, PVC, Service, Deployment |
| Stop | `POST /api/v1/agents/{id}/stop` — deletes Deployment only (PVC persists) |
| Patch | `PATCH /api/v1/agents/{id}` — agent must be STOPPED; bumps template version |
| Delete | `DELETE /api/v1/agents/{id}` — soft-delete in DB, hard-delete all k8s resources |

Patching markdown fields followed by start regenerates the ConfigMap with the
new content. Since `INIT_OPENCLAW_JS` always overwrites workspace files from
ConfigMap on boot, updates land on the PVC immediately — no manual cleanup.

---

## Verifying agent behavior

```bash
# Watch which agent pods exist
kubectl get pods -n agent-farm -l 'app' --watch

# Identify a specific agent's pod
kubectl get pods -n agent-farm -l app=agent-<UUID> -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}'

# Check that the init script seeded files this boot
kubectl logs -n agent-farm <pod-name> | head -20
# Expect: "[init-openclaw] Copied workspace/SOUL.md" lines + "Config merged successfully"

# Inspect the workspace files openclaw is actually reading
kubectl exec -n agent-farm <pod-name> -- cat /home/node/.openclaw/workspace/IDENTITY.md
```

---

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------|-----|
| `ErrImagePull` / `ImagePullBackOff` after switching to local image | `imagePullPolicy` still `Always`, or you forgot the `k3s ctr import` | Verify both: `kubectl get deploy ... -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].imagePullPolicy}'` and `sudo k3s crictl images \| grep <name>` |
| `Connection refused` to localhost:8000 | Port-forward died (api pod restarted) | Re-run `kubectl port-forward ...` |
| Agent doesn't respond to @mention | Two original gaps both fixed in code (`groupPolicy: open`, slack→main binding). If it regresses, check ConfigMap data `openclaw-config-overlay.json` |
| Agent says "Who am I?" on boot | Workspace markdown not seeded — confirm `INIT_OPENCLAW_JS` ran by checking pod logs for `[init-openclaw] Copied workspace/...` |

| UI shows **500 on login** | `NEXT_PUBLIC_BACKEND_URL` not passed at build time — rewrite points to `localhost:8000` (pod's own loopback) instead of `agentfarm-api:8000` | Rebuild with `docker build ... --build-arg NEXT_PUBLIC_BACKEND_URL=http://agentfarm-api:8000`; re-import; rollout restart |
| `kubectl` says "Unable to connect to the server" | Wrong kubeconfig (using the remote one without SSH tunnel?) or k3s isn't running | `systemctl status k3s` and verify `KUBECONFIG` points to `.k3s-local.yaml`; see the local vs remote table above |
| `kubectl` says "certificate signed by unknown authority" | Remote kubeconfig loaded but SSH tunnel not running | Start the tunnel (`ssh -N -L 6443:...`) or switch to `.k3s-local.yaml` |
| Patched deployment image reverts | Someone ran `helmfile sync` | Re-apply the local-image patch |

helmfile destroy
kubectl delete namespace agent-farm
# Full wipe (also removes k3s):

```

## Permanent fix for node-IP flips (local only)

**Problem:** DHCP changes the host LAN IP. The API pod's mounted kubeconfig (and the
`kubernetes` Service endpoints) bake the old node IP, so every flip makes the API pod's
calls to the apiserver time out (`ConnectTimeoutError ... :6443`) and agent start/stop hangs.

**Fix:** point the pod's kubeconfig at the **cni0 / flannel gateway `10.42.0.1`**, which is
the pod-network gateway — reachable from every pod and **stable across DHCP changes**
(the apiserver listens on `*:6443`). Production is unaffected: its kubeconfig comes from the
`POD_KUBECONFIG_B64` GitHub secret with static node IPs; never put `10.42.0.1` in git-tracked
helm/values or it would ship to prod.

1. Add `10.42.0.1` to k3s tls-san so CA verification still works:
   `/etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml` →
   ```yaml
   tls-san:
     - 10.42.0.1
   ```
   then `sudo rm /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/tls/serving-kube-apiserver.{crt,key}` and
   `sudo systemctl restart k3s` (regenerates the cert with the new SAN).
2. Source of truth: `miscellaneous/agent-farm-pod-kubeconfig.k3s-local.yaml` (gitignored) —
   same token, `server: https://10.42.0.1:6443`. The live secret is patched from it.
3. Re-applying after a `helmfile sync` (which recreates the secret from `POD_KUBECONFIG_B64`):
   ```bash
   export POD_KUBECONFIG_B64=$(base64 -w0 miscellaneous/agent-farm-pod-kubeconfig.k3s-local.yaml)
   helmfile sync   # or just patch the live secret + bounce the api pod
   ```

After this, LAN-IP flips no longer break the API↔apiserver path — no per-flip patching.

All of the secrets below are created as repository secrets in the current setup. The deploy workflows use staging/production secret pairs, but they do not require separate GitHub Environments.

## Sanity Checks

- `GCP_CREDENTIALS` must be valid raw JSON, not base64 unless your workflow decodes it.
- `KUBECONFIG_*` must contain the full kubeconfig YAML, not a filesystem path.
- `K8S_*` secrets are multiline dotenv blobs with one `KEY=value` per line.
- `KLIKT_*_ENV_CI` secrets are also full dotenv blobs.
- The backend config is strict. Missing required keys such as `LINKEDIN_APIFY_ACTOR_ID` will crash the API and worker pods at startup.
- If `google-github-actions/auth@v2` fails with “must specify exactly one of workload_identity_provider or credentials_json”, check that `GCP_CREDENTIALS` exists and is non-empty in the scope where the job runs.
- Secrets are not passed to workflows triggered from forks by default.
